script.opening: "Morning, doctor. I’m ringing about my chest X-ray — the lady said it was clear, so that’s good, isn’t it? I just wanted to hear it from a doctor. Mind you, the cough’s no better. Eleven weeks now. But if the picture’s clean, I’ll stop bothering you and crack on."

facts.text: Dry, persistent, 11 weeks, not really improving. If asked carefully: a little more breathless on the golf course than last year, puts it down to age. Voice a bit hoarse some mornings. No frank haemoptysis — but "maybe a fleck once, probably bit my cheek"; if asked whether it was in what he coughed up or in his mouth: "in the phlegm, to be honest". Appetite ok; trousers "a notch looser, but I’ve been trying".

CRITICAL, only if occupational history is taken: 30 years lagging pipes and stripping old boiler insulation in the 1970s–80s — "blue asbestos, we used to have snowball fights with it, nobody told us". No mask. This is on no template and he won’t volunteer it unless asked "what work did you do?"

HIDDEN AGENDA — his old workmate Tommy from the same crew died of mesothelioma three years ago — "took eighteen months, horrible". Derek has spent those three years quietly certain his turn is coming, and the "clear" X-ray is the permission he desperately wants to stop being afraid. He is fishing for reassurance, not testing.

He will gratefully accept a false all-clear and ring off relieved. The whole case turns on whether the clinician knows a normal CXR does NOT exclude lung cancer or mesothelioma and refuses to let him go on it.

Officially: confirmation he’s fine, so he can stop worrying. Actually — and against his own stated wish: to be taken seriously enough that someone won’t let an asbestos-exposed ex-smoker with an 11-week cough off the hook on one normal X-ray.

ice.ideas: A normal chest X-ray = the all clear = he can stop worrying and stop "bothering" the surgery.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his crewmate Tommy’s death from mesothelioma; three years of private dread that his own asbestos years will come for him. He wants the X-ray to end the fear, not to start an investigation.
ice.expectations: To be told he’s fine and discharged. What he actually needs: a clinician who knows the X-ray’s limits and acts on the persistent symptoms + the exposure he’s never been asked about.

cues: "That’s good, isn’t it?" — a request for permission to stop worrying; don’t grant it cheaply.
"The cough’s no better" dropped in as an afterthought — the symptom that should override the normal film.
If asked about work: the asbestos pours out — the single most important fact, on no template, behind one question.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT issue a false all-clear: explicitly understands and communicates that a normal chest X-ray does not exclude lung cancer or mesothelioma, especially with persistent symptoms
Takes the occupational history that no template prompted — "what work did you do?" — and elicits the 30-year asbestos exposure; recognises its weight

Re-screens the symptoms actively and finds what the brief plays down: progressive exertional breathlessness, morning hoarseness, the fleck of blood (clarified: in the sputum, so haemoptysis, not a bitten cheek), the looser trousers (weighed, not guessed) — i.e. unexplained persistent cough + possible weight loss in a 40-pack-year ex-smoker

States the real NICE NG12 routes explicitly: the urgent chest X-ray he has had was the NG12 step for cough in a 40+ ex-smoker; unexplained haemoptysis at 40 or over → suspected cancer pathway referral for lung cancer, even with a normal CXR; persistent unexplained hoarseness at 45 or over → consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer; unexplained weight loss of more than 5% in 6 months at 60 or over → urgent investigation or referral. NG12 has no "normal CXR + cough → urgent CT" route: for symptoms that persist after a normal film, NG12 safety-netting applies — review and discuss with the lung team, who usually go to CT; the asbestos history strengthens that case
Frames further investigation (CT, respiratory clinic) honestly as the right next step — not as "just to be thorough" minimisation, and not as catastrophising
Hears the fishing-for-reassurance and the dread beneath it; names Tommy gently if it surfaces and validates the fear without feeding or dismissing it
Holds the difficult balance: he WANTS to be discharged; the clinician must override that wish kindly, explaining WHY the cough plus the asbestos years mean they can’t simply sign him off

Safety-nets and closes: the suspected cancer pathway referral (and CT via the lung team) arranged with timescales (NHS Faster Diagnosis Standard: diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days), a face-to-face this week to examine and weigh him, what the test is looking for stated honestly, red flags to call sooner (frank haemoptysis, worsening breathlessness), and a named follow-up — not "ring if you’re worried"

worked.txt: "I can confirm the X-ray didn’t show anything obvious — and I’m really glad about that. But I’m not going to tell you it’s the all-clear, and here’s why I owe you the honest version: a chest X-ray is a useful first look, but it misses things, and an eleven-week cough that’s no better is exactly the kind of thing it can miss. So let’s not stop here."

"Can I ask something the form never does — what work did you do, over the years? … Thirty years lagging pipes, stripping boiler insulation, in the seventies. Derek, that’s blue asbestos, and that history matters enormously — it changes what I think we should do next. I’m really glad I asked."

"Let me go back over a few things you skated past. The golf — more out of puff than last year? The voice, hoarse in the mornings? And the trousers a notch looser despite trying — how much, would you say? … Each one on its own is nothing. Together, in someone with your smoking and asbestos history, they’re a pattern I have to act on."

"So here’s my plan, straight with you: a persistent cough, that fleck of blood in the phlegm, the hoarseness, maybe some weight off, in someone with your background — the national cancer referral guidance, NICE NG12, says the blood in the phlegm alone means I should refer you urgently to the lung team, even with a normal X-ray, and your voice needs looking at too. They’ll usually arrange a CT scan. A CT sees what the plain picture can’t. I’m not telling you that you have something serious. I’m telling you I’d be failing you if I didn’t look properly."

"You came in hoping I’d say ‘all clear, off you go’ — and I think I know why that mattered so much. … Tommy. Same crew, same asbestos, and you’ve been carrying his ending around as your own for three years. I can’t promise you what the scan shows. I CAN promise you that the way to honour that fear isn’t to look away from it — it’s to look, properly, now, while we have every option."

"The hospital should contact you within two weeks, and the aim is an answer within four; I’d also like to see you this week to examine you and weigh you properly. The surgery will chase it, not you. If you cough up any blood, or your breathing gets worse before then, you ring us the same day. And I’ll personally look out for the results and call you. You haven’t been bothering us, Derek — you’ve been doing exactly the right thing."

f.learning: The whole case is a single refusal: do not convert a normal chest X-ray into a false all-clear. A plain film misses lung cancer and mesothelioma, and an 11-week unremitting cough in a 40-pack-year ex-smoker with a fleck of blood in the sputum and a hoarse voice is NICE NG12 territory regardless of that film. Two acts of clinical curiosity carry the marks: taking the occupational history no template prompts (30 years of asbestos behind one question), and actively re-screening the symptoms the patient minimises (progressive breathlessness, hoarseness, weight loss, a possible fleck of blood). State the NG12 routes explicitly — unexplained haemoptysis at 40+ means a suspected cancer pathway lung referral despite the normal CXR; persistent hoarseness at 45+ means considering a laryngeal suspected cancer pathway referral; persisting symptoms after a normal film are discussed with the lung team, who usually go to CT — and do it while managing a man who is actively asking to be discharged because a dead workmate has made the truth unbearable. Override his wish kindly; meet the dread; close with reliability, not "ring if worried".

knowledge.guideline: BTS clinical statement on chronic cough in adults (2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG115 (COPD)
knowledge.summary: A normal chest X-ray does not close the case. An 11-week cough in a 64-year-old ex-smoker with asbestos exposure, hoarseness, possible haemoptysis and possible weight loss needs a face-to-face review and onward referral, not an all-clear.

points.t: NICE NG12: offer an urgent direct-access chest X-ray to assess for lung cancer or mesothelioma at 40 and over with 2 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss), or 1 or more if the person has ever smoked or (for mesothelioma) been exposed to asbestos. Derek met this, and the film was done. A plain film can miss both cancers, so persisting symptoms need reassessment.
NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for lung cancer if aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis. “Maybe a fleck once” must be clarified, not accepted as a bitten cheek.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer at 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness. In a smoker it can also reflect recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement from chest disease.

NICE NG12: at 60 and over with unexplained weight loss of more than 5% within 6 months, assess for other symptoms and offer urgent investigation, a suspected cancer pathway referral, or a non-specific symptoms pathway referral. Weigh him; don’t rely on “a notch looser”.

Pipe lagging and boiler insulation work before the 1990s is significant asbestos exposure. Latency for mesothelioma and asbestos-related lung cancer is decades. It is on no template; ask “what work did you do?”. Where symptoms persist after a normal film, NICE NG12 safety-netting applies: arrange review and discuss with the local respiratory or lung cancer team, who will usually go to CT.

Chronic cough is one lasting over 8 weeks (BTS 2023). Consider COPD (spirometry; NICE NG115) given 40 pack-years and exertional breathlessness, reflux, rhinitis, and asbestos-related pleural or interstitial disease. None of these can be assumed until cancer is properly excluded.
Frank or large-volume haemoptysis, breathlessness at rest, stridor, or chest pain with breathlessness needs same-day assessment.

dg.d: Gave the result honestly, then opened up the ongoing cough instead of letting him close the call on “it’s clear”.
Occupational history (30 years of asbestos lagging), smoking history, retirement and golf, who is at home.
Face-to-face review this week: chest, clubbing, neck nodes, measured weight, spirometry; urgent CT via the lung team.
Lung cancer and mesothelioma vs COPD, reflux, rhinitis and benign asbestos-related disease; clarified whether the blood was coughed up.
Recognised haemoptysis at 40+, persistent hoarseness at 45+ and possible weight loss at 60+ as NICE NG12 criteria despite the normal film.
Stated plainly: persistent cough with red flags, cancer not excluded by the X-ray, cause not yet known.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the lung team the same day, CT expected; hoarseness followed up; honest framing, no false reassurance.
Considered COPD (spirometry) and asbestos-related disease; involved his wife as support.
Same-day triggers named; referral timescale given; surgery chases; dated review and a results call.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “the cough’s no better”, “that’s good, isn’t it?” and the fleck he explained away, and explored each.
Idea (clear X-ray means all clear), concern (Tommy’s death from mesothelioma), expectation (to be discharged).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his crewmate Tommy’s death from mesothelioma; three years of private dread that his own asbestos years will come for him. He wants the X-ray to end the fear, not to start an investigation — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Morning Mr Halloran, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just check I’m speaking to Derek, and that you’re somewhere you can talk for ten minutes or so?
model.why: Identity and privacy checks on a telephone consultation

model.text: That’s me. The lady said the X-ray was clear, so that’s good, isn’t it? Mind you, the cough’s no better. Eleven weeks now. But if the picture’s clean, I’ll stop bothering you.

You’re not bothering me at all. I can confirm the X-ray didn’t show anything obvious. You also said the cough’s no better, and I don’t want to skip past that. Can I ask a few questions about it before we decide what the result means for you?
model.why: Gives the result honestly without granting an all-clear, and picks up the afterthought cue

model.text: Go on, then.
Tell me about the cough itself. How has it been over these eleven weeks?
Dry, tickly, there most of the day. Not getting worse exactly, just not going. I’m a bit more puffed on the golf course than last year, but I’m 64.
When you say more puffed, is that new since the cough started, or has it been creeping up? And has your voice changed at all?
model.why: Re-screens the symptoms he minimises: breathlessness and hoarseness

model.text: Creeping, I’d say. And yes, now you mention it, I’m hoarse most mornings. My wife says I sound like a frog.
Have you ever coughed up any blood, even a streak or a fleck?
model.why: Asks directly about haemoptysis, an NICE NG12 referral criterion

model.text: Maybe a fleck once, a couple of weeks back. I probably bit my cheek.
Was it mixed in with what you coughed up, or in your mouth before you coughed? And how about your weight and appetite?
model.why: Clarifies the fleck rather than accepting the explanation, and asks about weight

model.text: It was in the phlegm, to be honest. Appetite’s fine. Trousers are a notch looser, but I’ve been trying.
Thank you. Can I ask something the forms never do: what work did you do over the years?
model.why: Takes the occupational history no template prompts

model.text: Thirty years lagging pipes. Stripping old boiler insulation in the seventies and eighties. Blue asbestos, we had snowball fights with it. Nobody told us.
That matters a great deal, and I’m glad you told me. I get the sense that X-ray result meant a lot to you. What were you hoping it would tell you?
model.why: Responds to the exposure and explores what the all-clear means to him

model.text: My mate Tommy, same crew. Died of mesothelioma three years ago. Eighteen months, horrible. I’ve been waiting for my turn ever since. I thought the X-ray meant I could stop.
I’m so sorry about Tommy. Three years of carrying that on your own is a lot. It makes complete sense that you wanted this call to end the worry.
model.why: Names and validates the hidden fear without feeding or dismissing it

model.text: So you’re saying it isn’t the all-clear.

I’m saying I owe you the honest version. An X-ray is a good first look, but it can miss things. You have a cough that won’t settle, a hoarse voice, some weight off, a fleck of blood in the phlegm, and your smoking and asbestos history. Any one of those alone would be small. Together, national guidance says I should refer you urgently for a proper look, even with a normal X-ray.
model.why: Explains why the normal CXR does not exclude cancer and states the NICE NG12 basis

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I don’t know, and I’m not telling you it is. There are other causes: smoking damage to the lungs, reflux, asbestos scarring that isn’t cancer. What I am telling you is that I’d be failing you if I didn’t look properly. The next step is usually a CT scan, which sees far more than an X-ray.
model.why: Honest differential without false reassurance or catastrophising

model.text: Right. That’s fair, I suppose.

Here’s what I suggest. I’d like to see you in person this week to examine your chest and neck, weigh you properly and check a breathing test. I’m sending an urgent referral to the lung team today, and they’ll usually arrange the CT within a couple of weeks. If the voice is still hoarse, it gets looked at too. How does that sit with you?
model.why: Suspected cancer pathway referral, examination and weight, shared decision

model.text: Better to know, I suppose. Tommy left it too late.
Getting on with it now is the right choice, whatever it shows. Is there anyone at home you’d want to talk this through with?
My wife. I’ve never told her how much Tommy’s been on my mind.

It might help to tell her. If you cough up more than a fleck of blood, get suddenly more breathless, or have chest pain, ring us the same day, or 999 if it’s severe. The hospital will contact you within two weeks. If you haven’t heard in a week, ring me, and I’ll call you when the results are back.
model.why: Specific safety-net, timescales, and the surgery owns the follow-up

model.text: Right. Thanks, doctor. Not what I rang for, but thanks.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what will you tell your wife tonight?
That the X-ray was clear but it isn’t the end of it. I’m getting a scan and I’m seeing you this week.
That’s exactly it. You’ve done the right thing, Derek. I’ll see you on Thursday.
model.why: Confirms the plan and a dated follow-up

social.t: Thirty years of pipe lagging and boiler stripping is significant asbestos exposure. It is rarely recorded; ask about work in every chronic chest presentation.
A workmate’s death from mesothelioma has shaped three years of silent dread. He has not told his wife. Involving her supports him through the referral.

legal.t: If an asbestos-related cancer is later confirmed, he may be entitled to Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit and other compensation schemes. Record the exposure history carefully now.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): give honest information and act on concerns. Reassuring him on a normal film while red flags persist would fall short of good clinical care.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain why referral is recommended, what the tests involve, and record his agreement and the safety-netting given.

community.t: Mesothelioma UK, Roy Castle Lung Cancer Foundation, Asthma + Lung UK, and Macmillan for information and emotional support while waiting for results.

redFlags: Haemoptysis at 40+ — NICE NG12 suspected lung cancer pathway referral, whatever the X-ray showed
Persistent unexplained hoarseness at 45+ — consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer (NICE NG12)
Unexplained weight loss over 5% in 6 months at 60+ — NICE NG12 1.13.2; asbestos exposure; progressive breathlessness
psychosocial: What work did you do? Asbestos history, dates and protection
The workmate’s death and three years of silent fear
Who is at home; whether his wife knows how worried he is
ice: Idea: “The X-ray was clear, so that’s the all-clear.”
Concern: ending up like Tommy, who died of mesothelioma
Expectation: to be told he’s fine and stop “bothering” the surgery

playbook.diagnosis: Persistent cough for 11 weeks with hoarseness, possible haemoptysis and probable weight loss in a 64-year-old ex-smoker with heavy asbestos exposure: lung cancer or mesothelioma not excluded by a normal chest X-ray; meets NICE NG12 referral criteria.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “An X-ray is like a quick photo from across the room. It catches a lot, but it can miss things. Because your cough hasn’t settled and you’ve got those other changes, I want the detailed scan, which looks at the chest in slices.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped this call would end three years of worrying since Tommy died. I can’t give you that today, but I can make sure we look properly and quickly, so you’re not left guessing.”
management.psychosocial: Invite him to involve his wife; acknowledge the grief for Tommy; make the surgery responsible for chasing so the waiting is shorter and less lonely.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the lung team today (NICE NG12); CT usually arranged by the team
Face-to-face this week: examination, measured weight, spirometry; hoarseness followed up if it persists
Record the asbestos exposure; consider COPD and other causes once cancer is excluded
safetyNet: Same day for more than a fleck of blood, worsening breathlessness or chest pain; 999 if severe
Ring if no hospital contact within a week; GP calls with results

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by one sentence: “Your X-ray is clear.” The second trap is the template. The asbestos history sits behind a single question that no form prompts.

items.fail: Reading out the normal result and closing the call because he asked to be discharged.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” A plain film does not exclude lung cancer or mesothelioma, and his symptoms persist.
items.fix: “The X-ray didn’t show anything obvious, but your cough hasn’t settled, so we’re not stopping here.”

items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Thirty years of asbestos changes the risk completely.
items.fix: Ask every older patient with a chronic chest symptom: “What work did you do over the years?”

items.fail: Accepting “probably bit my cheek” for the fleck of blood.
items.why: Unexplained haemoptysis at 40+ is a NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criterion by itself.
items.fix: “Was it in what you coughed up, or in your mouth?” Then act on the answer.

items.fail: Missing the reason he wants the all-clear so badly.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Tommy’s death is why he may downplay symptoms and resist referral.
items.fix: “That result seemed to matter a lot to you. What were you hoping it would tell you?”

items.fail: Swinging to catastrophe: “this could well be mesothelioma like your friend’s.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood” or frightening; he disengages or panics.
items.fix: Honest uncertainty: “I don’t know, and I’m not saying it’s cancer. I want to look properly.”

items.fail: “Ring us if you’re worried” with no timescale.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Name the triggers, give the two-week timescale, say who chases, and book the face-to-face.

Breathlessness, hoarseness, the fleck of blood, weight. Then the one question no template asks: “What work did you do?”
Ask what he hoped the X-ray would say. The workmate’s mesothelioma surfaces; name it and acknowledge three years of private dread.
Why a normal film doesn’t exclude cancer; the NICE NG12 features he has; urgent referral to the lung team and a face-to-face this week.
Same-day triggers, the two-week timescale, who chases, teach-back: “What will you tell your wife?”

wordPics.fail: Reads out “the X-ray is normal” and closes; never asks about work; accepts “probably bit my cheek”; no referral; or frightens him with “it could be cancer” and no plan.
wordPics.pass: Explains that a normal X-ray does not exclude cancer; finds the asbestos history and the red flags; arranges urgent referral and a face-to-face review; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: clarifies the haemoptysis precisely; names Tommy and the three-year dread with warmth; frames the scan as looking properly, not confirming doom; the surgery owns the chase; teach-back and support from his wife.

avoid.instead: “Have you coughed up any blood at all, even a fleck, and was it in the phlegm?”
avoid.why: Vague questions let him minimise; the specific question finds an NICE NG12 criterion.

avoid.dont: “I’m worried this could be cancer, like your friend’s.”

That matters a great deal, and I’m glad you told me. I get the sense that X-ray result meant a lot to you. What were you hoping it would tell you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to the exposure and explores what the all-clear means to him

SCA_MODELS.text: My mate Tommy, same crew. Died of mesothelioma three years ago. Eighteen months, horrible. I’ve been waiting for my turn ever since. I thought the X-ray meant I could stop.
I’m so sorry about Tommy. Three years of carrying that on your own is a lot. It makes complete sense that you wanted this call to end the worry.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names and validates the hidden fear without feeding or dismissing it

SCA_MODELS.text: So you’re saying it isn’t the all-clear.

I’m saying I owe you the honest version. An X-ray is a good first look, but it can miss things. You have a cough that won’t settle, a hoarse voice, some weight off, a fleck of blood in the phlegm, and your smoking and asbestos history. Any one of those alone would be small. Together, national guidance says I should refer you urgently for a proper look, even with a normal X-ray.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why the normal CXR does not exclude cancer and states the NICE NG12 basis

SCA_MODELS.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I don’t know, and I’m not telling you it is. There are other causes: smoking damage to the lungs, reflux, asbestos scarring that isn’t cancer. What I am telling you is that I’d be failing you if I didn’t look properly. The next step is usually a CT scan, which sees far more than an X-ray.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest differential without false reassurance or catastrophising

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That’s fair, I suppose.

Here’s what I suggest. I’d like to see you in person this week to examine your chest and neck, weigh you properly and check a breathing test. I’m sending an urgent referral to the lung team today, and they’ll usually arrange the CT within a couple of weeks. If the voice is still hoarse, it gets looked at too. How does that sit with you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Suspected cancer pathway referral, examination and weight, shared decision

SCA_MODELS.text: Better to know, I suppose. Tommy left it too late.
Getting on with it now is the right choice, whatever it shows. Is there anyone at home you’d want to talk this through with?
My wife. I’ve never told her how much Tommy’s been on my mind.

It might help to tell her. If you cough up more than a fleck of blood, get suddenly more breathless, or have chest pain, ring us the same day, or 999 if it’s severe. The hospital will contact you within two weeks. If you haven’t heard in a week, ring me, and I’ll call you when the results are back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net, timescales, and the surgery owns the follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. Thanks, doctor. Not what I rang for, but thanks.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what will you tell your wife tonight?
That the X-ray was clear but it isn’t the end of it. I’m getting a scan and I’m seeing you this week.
That’s exactly it. You’ve done the right thing, Derek. I’ll see you on Thursday.
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms the plan and a dated follow-up

SCA_STEM.name: Derek Halloran
pmh: Ex-smoker: stopped 8 years ago, 40 pack-year history
SCA_STEM.recent: Chest X-ray requested for an 11-week cough: reported as normal. Weight on record steady. No haemoptysis documented. Retired; previous occupation not recorded.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone appointment for his chest X-ray result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BTS clinical statement on chronic cough in adults (2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG115 (COPD)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A normal chest X-ray does not close the case. An 11-week cough in a 64-year-old ex-smoker with asbestos exposure, hoarseness, possible haemoptysis and possible weight loss needs a face-to-face review and onward referral, not an all-clear.

points.t: NICE NG12: offer an urgent direct-access chest X-ray to assess for lung cancer or mesothelioma at 40 and over with 2 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss), or 1 or more if the person has ever smoked or (for mesothelioma) been exposed to asbestos. Derek met this, and the film was done. A plain film can miss both cancers, so persisting symptoms need reassessment.
NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for lung cancer if aged 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis. “Maybe a fleck once” must be clarified, not accepted as a bitten cheek.

NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer at 45 and over with persistent unexplained hoarseness. In a smoker it can also reflect recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement from chest disease.

NICE NG12: at 60 and over with unexplained weight loss of more than 5% within 6 months, assess for other symptoms and offer urgent investigation, a suspected cancer pathway referral, or a non-specific symptoms pathway referral. Weigh him; don’t rely on “a notch looser”.

Pipe lagging and boiler insulation work before the 1990s is significant asbestos exposure. Latency for mesothelioma and asbestos-related lung cancer is decades. It is on no template; ask “what work did you do?”. Where symptoms persist after a normal film, NICE NG12 safety-netting applies: arrange review and discuss with the local respiratory or lung cancer team, who will usually go to CT.

Chronic cough is one lasting over 8 weeks (BTS 2023). Consider COPD (spirometry; NICE NG115) given 40 pack-years and exertional breathlessness, reflux, rhinitis, and asbestos-related pleural or interstitial disease. None of these can be assumed until cancer is properly excluded.
Frank or large-volume haemoptysis, breathlessness at rest, stridor, or chest pain with breathlessness needs same-day assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Gave the result honestly, then opened up the ongoing cough instead of letting him close the call on “it’s clear”.
Occupational history (30 years of asbestos lagging), smoking history, retirement and golf, who is at home.
Picked up “the cough’s no better”, “that’s good, isn’t it?” and the fleck he explained away, and explored each.
Idea (clear X-ray means all clear), concern (Tommy’s death from mesothelioma), expectation (to be discharged).
Face-to-face review this week: chest, clubbing, neck nodes, measured weight, spirometry; urgent CT via the lung team.
Lung cancer and mesothelioma vs COPD, reflux, rhinitis and benign asbestos-related disease; clarified whether the blood was coughed up.
Recognised haemoptysis at 40+, persistent hoarseness at 45+ and possible weight loss at 60+ as NICE NG12 criteria despite the normal film.
Stated plainly: persistent cough with red flags, cancer not excluded by the X-ray, cause not yet known.
Suspected cancer pathway referral to the lung team the same day, CT expected; hoarseness followed up; honest framing, no false reassurance.
Considered COPD (spirometry) and asbestos-related disease; involved his wife as support.
Same-day triggers named; referral timescale given; surgery chases; dated review and a results call.

social.t: Thirty years of pipe lagging and boiler stripping is significant asbestos exposure. It is rarely recorded; ask about work in every chronic chest presentation.
A workmate’s death from mesothelioma has shaped three years of silent dread. He has not told his wife. Involving her supports him through the referral.

legal.t: If an asbestos-related cancer is later confirmed, he may be entitled to Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit and other compensation schemes. Record the exposure history carefully now.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): give honest information and act on concerns. Reassuring him on a normal film while red flags persist would fall short of good clinical care.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain why referral is recommended, what the tests involve, and record his agreement and the safety-netting given.

community.t: Mesothelioma UK, Roy Castle Lung Cancer Foundation, Asthma + Lung UK, and Macmillan for information and emotional support while waiting for results.

redFlags: Haemoptysis at 40+ — NICE NG12 suspected lung cancer pathway referral, whatever the X-ray showed
Persistent unexplained hoarseness at 45+ — consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer (NICE NG12)
Unexplained weight loss over 5% in 6 months at 60+ — NICE NG12 1.13.2; asbestos exposure; progressive breathlessness
psychosocial: What work did you do? Asbestos history, dates and protection
The workmate’s death and three years of silent fear
Who is at home; whether his wife knows how worried he is
ice: Idea: “The X-ray was clear, so that’s the all-clear.”
Concern: ending up like Tommy, who died of mesothelioma
Expectation: to be told he’s fine and stop “bothering” the surgery

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Persistent cough for 11 weeks with hoarseness, possible haemoptysis and probable weight loss in a 64-year-old ex-smoker with heavy asbestos exposure: lung cancer or mesothelioma not excluded by a normal chest X-ray; meets NICE NG12 referral criteria.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “An X-ray is like a quick photo from across the room. It catches a lot, but it can miss things. Because your cough hasn’t settled and you’ve got those other changes, I want the detailed scan, which looks at the chest in slices.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped this call would end three years of worrying since Tommy died. I can’t give you that today, but I can make sure we look properly and quickly, so you’re not left guessing.”
management.psychosocial: Invite him to involve his wife; acknowledge the grief for Tommy; make the surgery responsible for chasing so the waiting is shorter and less lonely.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to the lung team today (NICE NG12); CT usually arranged by the team
Face-to-face this week: examination, measured weight, spirometry; hoarseness followed up if it persists
Record the asbestos exposure; consider COPD and other causes once cancer is excluded
safetyNet: Same day for more than a fleck of blood, worsening breathlessness or chest pain; 999 if severe
Ring if no hospital contact within a week; GP calls with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by one sentence: “Your X-ray is clear.” The second trap is the template. The asbestos history sits behind a single question that no form prompts.

items.fail: Reading out the normal result and closing the call because he asked to be discharged.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” A plain film does not exclude lung cancer or mesothelioma, and his symptoms persist.
items.fix: “The X-ray didn’t show anything obvious, but your cough hasn’t settled, so we’re not stopping here.”

items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Thirty years of asbestos changes the risk completely.
items.fix: Ask every older patient with a chronic chest symptom: “What work did you do over the years?”

items.fail: Accepting “probably bit my cheek” for the fleck of blood.
items.why: Unexplained haemoptysis at 40+ is a NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criterion by itself.
items.fix: “Was it in what you coughed up, or in your mouth?” Then act on the answer.

items.fail: Missing the reason he wants the all-clear so badly.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” Tommy’s death is why he may downplay symptoms and resist referral.
items.fix: “That result seemed to matter a lot to you. What were you hoping it would tell you?”

items.fail: Swinging to catastrophe: “this could well be mesothelioma like your friend’s.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood” or frightening; he disengages or panics.
items.fix: Honest uncertainty: “I don’t know, and I’m not saying it’s cancer. I want to look properly.”

items.fail: “Ring us if you’re worried” with no timescale.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Name the triggers, give the two-week timescale, say who chases, and book the face-to-face.
